title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
hook: a kid tears a page in half, and in half again, and Vaisheshika asks where the tearing has to stop

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika, the school of Kanada, opened with dharma and with vishesha: each thing is itself. Now, the atoms.
screen: `VISHESHA: EACH THING IS ITSELF.` · `NOW, THE ATOMS.`

segments.voice: A kid at the kitchen table has a sheet of paper and a serious expression. She tears it in half. Then one half in half. Then that half. The pieces get smaller and her fingers clumsier, until she's pinching a scrap you can barely see. "Can I keep going?" she asks. "Forever?" The grown-up across the table just shrugs. Vaisheshika had an answer. Not forever. Somewhere down there the tearing has to stop, at something so small it has no halves left to tear. The school gave that something a name, and the name became the idea the school is known for.
screen: `TEARING A PAGE IN HALF.` → `CAN I KEEP GOING FOREVER?` → `NO: THE TEARING STOPS.`

segments.voice: The name is paramanu, often translated atom: the smallest of the small. A paramanu has no parts, so it can't come apart, and Vaisheshika calls it eternal: it can't be made and it can't be destroyed. You can't see one, either. So why believe in it? The school's thinkers gave an argument. If you could divide forever, a mountain would have endless parts, and so would a mustard seed. Then what makes the mountain bigger? So the dividing must stop somewhere, at a partless thing. That's an inference, the kind of step Nyaya says out loud. In the classic account the commentators give, atoms join in a ladder. Two atoms pair up. Then pairs gather, and you reach the smallest thing an eye can see: a speck of dust floating in a beam of sunlight. From there, upward, to clay and rivers and mountains. There are atoms of earth, of water, of fire, of air, each kind carrying its own qualities. Everything you can see is made of parts. Everything made of parts, sooner or later, comes apart: the cup, the house, the body. But what it's made of doesn't vanish. The pieces go back down the ladder and wait. That's an unusual kind of comfort. Vaisheshika doesn't say nothing is lost. It says the breaking happens in the joints, not at the bottom of things.
screen: `PARAMANU: THE SMALLEST OF THE SMALL.` · `NO PARTS, SO IT NEVER COMES APART.` · `A MOUNTAIN AND A MUSTARD SEED.` · `A SPECK IN A SUNBEAM.` · then, large: `THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.`

segments.voice: Let your attention move through your body as an assembly of parts: hands, shoulders, the back against the chair, the feet on the floor. Then hold one thing that has come apart lately, a plan, a routine, maybe something more, without fixing it, and notice that what it was made of, the effort, the care, the time, hasn't simply disappeared. If you pray, you can rest in what you trust does not come apart.
Vaisheshika. The school of particulars and of the paramanu: the partless smallest thing, which never comes apart, where all dividing has to stop.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. What things are made of goes back down the ladder and waits. That's day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn the teaching on atoms through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries, usually alongside Nyaya, as part of traditional Sanskrit study.

trapdoor: what you thought: atoms are a modern idea.
what it means: Vaisheshika reasoned its way to partless, eternal paramanus, so that what breaks comes apart at the joints, not at the bottom.
what a scholar hears: in the classic Vaisheshika account, atoms combine as dyads, then triads, the triad being the smallest visible thing, a mote in a sunbeam.

chat.says: Can you cut something in half forever, or does it stop?
options: Vaisheshika says it stops at the paramanu, a partless thing that never comes apart.
Vaisheshika says it stops at a speck in a sunbeam, the smallest thing there is.
Vaisheshika says it stops at earth, water, fire and air, which can't be split at all.
chat.meaning: If dividing never stopped, a mountain and a mustard seed would both have endless parts. So Vaisheshika infers partless, eternal paramanus.

paramanu.meaning: the partless smallest thing, often translated atom

Paramanu glossed 'the smallest of the small' (parama + anu): lexical; confirm.

The mountain/mustard-seed argument against infinite divisibility is attributed to 'the school's thinkers'; confirm the source (commentarial; also discussed around Nyaya Sutra 4.2).

Dyad/triad ladder and the mote in a sunbeam (trasarenu) are attributed to 'the classic account the commentators give' (Prashastapada and later); the spoken text gives pairs but no count for the triad; trapdoor floor 3 names dyads and triads. Confirm.
Atoms of earth, water, fire and air: confirm (akasha is not atomic in Vaisheshika).
